explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Habakkuk says, "O LORD, You have appointed them to execute judgment…" (Habakkuk 1:12). He's talking about the Chaldeans, the nation the LORD said He was raising up (Habakkuk 1:6). Habakkuk gets the word right even while he's wrestling with what it means.

Close to the neighborhood, friend, but no. The word Habakkuk uses is judgment (Habakkuk 1:12). Mercy actually shows up in his very last question of this passage, where he asks if the foe will keep slaying nations "without mercy" (Habakkuk 1:17). So mercy is in the passage, just not in this verse.

Nope, worship isn't what the LORD appointed them for. Habakkuk says He appointed them to execute judgment and established them for correction (Habakkuk 1:12). Worship does come up later, but it's the foe worshiping his own nets (Habakkuk 1:16). That's a whole different kind of worship, baker.

True, baker. Habakkuk says it right there in the middle of his prayer: "We will not die." (Habakkuk 1:12). He says it just after calling the LORD his God and his Holy One, and just before he starts asking the hard questions. I think that's a man who has a lot on his mind and still knows where to stand.

I get why it sounds too bold, friend, but the text has him saying it. Habakkuk 1:12 reads, "We will not die." Those words come right after he calls the LORD his God and his Holy One. So this one is true, and those words are in his prayer.

explanations.answer: Why He's silent as the wicked swallow those more righteous
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! Habakkuk asks, "Why are You silent while the wicked swallow up those more righteous than themselves?" (Habakkuk 1:13). He asks it straight out, with no sneaking around the question. I think that's the kind of honest question a person only asks someone they trust.

explanations.answer: Why He made the horses of the Chaldeans so swift
explanations.explanation: Interesting guess, friend, but that's not what Habakkuk asks here. Right after saying the LORD's eyes are too pure to look upon evil, he asks, "So why do You tolerate the faithless?" and why the LORD is silent while the wicked swallow up those more righteous (Habakkuk 1:13). His question is about the LORD tolerating and being silent. Nobody's asking for horse specs.

explanations.answer: Why He chose a prophet from such a small town
explanations.explanation: Ha, that's a question for a different kind of day, baker. This passage never mentions Habakkuk's hometown at all. What he asks is why the LORD tolerates the faithless and stays silent while the wicked swallow up those more righteous (Habakkuk 1:13). The text keeps his question on the wicked, not on himself.
That's the one, baker. "The foe pulls all of them up with a hook…" says Habakkuk 1:15. Then come the dragnet and the fishing net too. The whole picture is a fisherman's, and the people are the catch.

A sword would make sense in a battle, friend, but this is a fishing picture. The text says the foe pulls them up with a hook, then catches them in a dragnet and gathers them in a fishing net (Habakkuk 1:15). Every tool in the verse is fishing gear. Swords stay home for this one.

A bow is a fair guess, baker, but it's not in the verse. Habakkuk 1:15 stays with fishing gear: a hook, a dragnet and a fishing net. The picture is people being pulled up like fish. I'll admit, a fisherman with a bow would be a lot of work for one fish.

Not quite, friend. After the hook, the dragnet and the fishing net, Habakkuk 1:15 says, "so he rejoices gladly." The text says he rejoices, and it never says he feels sorry for his catch. I think that's exactly what troubles Habakkuk so much.

False is right, baker. Habakkuk 1:15 says the foe pulls them up with a hook, catches them in his dragnet and gathers them in his fishing net, "so he rejoices gladly." No sorry in sight. He's glad about his haul.

explanations.answer: Sacrifices and burns incense to them
explanations.explanation: Right on, baker. Habakkuk 1:16 says, "Therefore he sacrifices to his dragnet and burns incense to his fishing net…" He treats his nets like they deserve a ceremony. The verse goes on to say that by these things his portion is sumptuous and his food is rich.

explanations.answer: Trades them for silver and gold
explanations.explanation: Good business instinct, friend, but the nets aren't for sale in this verse. The text says he sacrifices to his dragnet and burns incense to his fishing net (Habakkuk 1:16). Silver and gold never come up in these verses. The nets stay with him, and he honors them.

explanations.answer: Lends them to the other nations
explanations.explanation: Nice of you to imagine him sharing, baker, but that's not in the text. Habakkuk 1:16 says he sacrifices to his dragnet and burns incense to his fishing net. And the verse says his portion is sumptuous by these things. Nothing about lending, just a lot of honoring.

explanations.answer: At his guard post on the ramparts
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Habakkuk says, "I will stand at my guard post and station myself on the ramparts." (Habakkuk 2:1). Then he says he'll watch to see what the LORD will say to him. I think that's a man who plans to stay put until he gets an answer.

explanations.answer: In the temple courts in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Reasonable guess, friend, but this passage never puts Habakkuk in the temple. He says, "I will stand at my guard post and station myself on the ramparts." (Habakkuk 2:1). Ramparts are the walls. So the place he names is up high, not in the temple courts.

explanations.answer: In a cave on Mount Horeb
explanations.explanation: That's a long hike for this one, baker. In Habakkuk 2:1 he says he will stand at his guard post and station himself on the ramparts. There's no cave and no mountain in these verses. He says he will watch to see what the LORD will say to him.

It's actually the opposite, friend. The LORD says, "Write down this vision and clearly inscribe it on tablets, so that a herald may run with it." (Habakkuk 2:2). A herald running with it means it's meant to get out there. I spent years stuck in the back of a junk drawer, and believe me, this vision is not meant for a drawer.

False is right, baker. The LORD tells Habakkuk, "Write down this vision and clearly inscribe it on tablets, so that a herald may run with it." (Habakkuk 2:2). It's to be written down clearly, and the purpose is for a herald to run with it. Nothing about keeping it to himself.
Yes, baker! The LORD says the vision is written "…so that a herald may run with it." (Habakkuk 2:2). A herald is someone who carries a message to others. That's why the writing has to be clear.

That's the second blank, baker. The herald "…may run with it." (Habakkuk 2:2). The picture is a messenger running with the message in hand. And the LORD says to inscribe it clearly so that this can happen.

A king is a fine title, friend, but it's not the word in the verse. The LORD says the vision is inscribed so that a herald may run with it (Habakkuk 2:2). A herald is the one who carries a message. Kings usually have somebody else do the running.

Stay is the opposite of what the verse says, baker. The LORD says the vision is written so that a herald may run with it (Habakkuk 2:2). The vision is meant to travel. And I wouldn't want to be the herald who stayed put with a message that big.

Nothing is hidden here, friend. The LORD says, "Write down this vision and clearly inscribe it on tablets, so that a herald may run with it." (Habakkuk 2:2). Clearly written, and carried by someone running. That's the opposite of hiding.

explanations.answer: Wait for it because it will surely come
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The LORD says, "Though it lingers, wait for it, since it will surely come and will not delay." (Habakkuk 2:3). It may feel slow, but the text says it will come. Waiting is hard work, and I know it myself from my years waiting in the back of a dark junk drawer.

explanations.answer: Write it again in bigger letters
explanations.explanation: Nice thinking, friend, but the LORD doesn't say that. He already told Habakkuk to write the vision down and inscribe it clearly (Habakkuk 2:2). Then about the delay He says, "Though it lingers, wait for it…" (Habakkuk 2:3). So the answer is waiting, not bigger letters.

explanations.answer: Ask another prophet for a new one
explanations.explanation: No second opinion needed, baker. The LORD says, "Though it lingers, wait for it, since it will surely come and will not delay." (Habakkuk 2:3). He also says the vision does not lie. So Habakkuk is told to wait for this one, not shop around.

You got it, baker. The LORD says, "…the righteous will live by faith…" (Habakkuk 2:4). It's set right beside the proud one, whose soul is not upright. Two very different people, and the verse tells you what the righteous one lives by.

Wealth is actually on the other side of this verse, friend. The text says wealth indeed betrays the proud one (Habakkuk 2:5). The righteous, the LORD says, will live by faith (Habakkuk 2:4). So faith is the answer, not wealth.
That's not what the verse says, baker. Right beside the proud one, the LORD says, "…the righteous will live by faith…" (Habakkuk 2:4). Strength isn't mentioned in it. Faith is the word the LORD uses.
